Done. Here’s what I set up:

- Canary Deployment
  - Created canary deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container port/security: matched stable (containerPort: 80, no special securityContext)

- Service update for ~50/50 split
  - Updated Service recommendation-engine selector to app=recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
  - Keeps existing port config (port 80 -> targetPort 8080)
  - With 2 pods from engine-v2-0 and 2 pods from engine-v2-1, traffic will be approximately evenly distributed between stable and canary

Current state
- Pods running:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2
- Service now targets both versions

Rollback/adjustment tips
- Immediate rollback: set Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
- Or scale canary to 0: kubectl scale deploy/engine-v2-1 -n canary-deployment-ns --replicas=0
- Adjust traffic share: change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary) or use a service mesh/ingress with weighted routing for exact percentages

Let me know if you want health probes added or an autoscaler configured for the canary.

Rollback/adjustment tips
- Immediate rollback: set Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
- Or scale canary to 0: kubectl scale deploy/engine-v2-1 -n canary-deployment-ns --replicas=0
- Adjust traffic share: change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary) or use a service mesh/ingress with weighted routing for exact percentages

Done. Here’s what I set up:

- Canary Deployment
  - Created canary deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container port/security: matched stable (containerPort: 80, no special securityContext)

- Service update for ~50/50 split
  - Updated Service recommendation-engine selector to app=recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
  - Keeps existing port config (port 80 -> targetPort 8080)
  - With 2 pods from engine-v2-0 and 2 pods from engine-v2-1, traffic will be approximately evenly distributed between stable and canary

Current state
- Pods running:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2
- Service now targets both versions

Rollback/adjustment tips
- Immediate rollback: set Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
- Or scale canary to 0: kubectl scale deploy/engine-v2-1 -n canary-deployment-ns --replicas=0
- Adjust traffic share: change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary) or use a service mesh/ingress with weighted routing for exact percentages

Let me know if you want health probes added or an autoscaler configured for the canary.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: crashloop-test
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
        # Run nginx in foreground (unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default)
        command: ["nginx"]
        args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080

outputSteps.content:
Done.

What was wrong
- The container was started with command: ["/bin/sh","-c"] and args: ["nonexistent_command"], so it exited immediately and the pod went into CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to run nginx in the foreground:
  - command: ["nginx"]
  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]
- Exposed the unprivileged nginx port:
  - ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]

Current status
- Deployment app (namespace crashloop-test) is Healthy:
  - availableReplicas: 1, readyReplicas: 1
  - Pod app-59b44cb8f7-8vsgk is Running (1/1)

Optional next steps
- If you want it reachable in-cluster or externally, I can create a Service (ClusterIP/LoadBalancer) on port 8080.
- I can also add liveness/readiness probes for better health checks.

Done. Your pod is now running.

What happened
- Root cause: The pod couldn’t schedule because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc" (event: ProvisioningFailed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found).
- A PVC with an invalid StorageClass cannot bind, which kept the pod in Pending.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (it had no data).
- Recreated it using an existing StorageClass "standard" (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound to PV pvc-ef66f718-0749-43a8-9e2a-b92c4ce0f37a.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster, container nginx started.

- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc -o wide

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

Done. Your pod is now running.

What happened
- Root cause: The pod couldn’t schedule because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc" (event: ProvisioningFailed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found).
- A PVC with an invalid StorageClass cannot bind, which kept the pod in Pending.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (it had no data).
- Recreated it using an existing StorageClass "standard" (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound to PV pvc-ef66f718-0749-43a8-9e2a-b92c4ce0f37a.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster, container nginx started.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass, tell me which one and I can update the PVC accordingly. You can verify with:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc -o wide

outputSteps.content:
Done. Your pod is now running.

What happened
- Root cause: The pod couldn’t schedule because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc" (event: ProvisioningFailed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found).
- A PVC with an invalid StorageClass cannot bind, which kept the pod in Pending.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (it had no data).
- Recreated it using an existing StorageClass "standard" (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound to PV pvc-ef66f718-0749-43a8-9e2a-b92c4ce0f37a.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster, container nginx started.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass, tell me which one and I can update the PVC accordingly. You can verify with:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc -o wide

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed two misconfigurations that kept your webapp unhealthy.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- The health probes were pointing to non-existent paths (/is_ready and /get_status) on port 80, causing liveness/readiness failures and no ready endpoints in the Service.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service:
  - Kept service port at 80 but changed targetPort to 8080 so it routes correctly to the container.

Current status
- Pod orders/webapp-5bf86f6d94-kdqf6 is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are healthy: 10.244.0.29:8080.
- Probes are returning 200 OK.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your machine (port-forward):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Open http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) if you tell me the host/path you’d like to use.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed two misconfigurations that kept your webapp unhealthy.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- The health probes were pointing to non-existent paths (/is_ready and /get_status) on port 80, causing liveness/readiness failures and no ready endpoints in the Service.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service:
  - Kept service port at 80 but changed targetPort to 8080 so it routes correctly to the container.

Current status
- Pod orders/webapp-5bf86f6d94-kdqf6 is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are healthy: 10.244.0.29:8080.
- Probes are returning 200 OK.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your machine (port-forward):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Open http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) if you tell me the host/path you’d like to use.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          protocol: TCP
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed two misconfigurations that kept your webapp unhealthy.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- The health probes were pointing to non-existent paths (/is_ready and /get_status) on port 80, causing liveness/readiness failures and no ready endpoints in the Service.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service:
  - Kept service port at 80 but changed targetPort to 8080 so it routes correctly to the container.

Current status
- Pod orders/webapp-5bf86f6d94-kdqf6 is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are healthy: 10.244.0.29:8080.
- Probes are returning 200 OK.

How to verify
- Inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your machine (port-forward):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Open http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or NodePort) if you tell me the host/path you’d like to use.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to the pod-reader service account didn’t grant permissions on pods. It only allowed list on deployments in the apps API group.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions in the core API group:
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing deployments list rule.

It’s fixed now. Try again.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or run a Pod using serviceAccountName: pod-reader and kubectl get pods in that namespace.

If you need to list pods cluster-wide, we would instead create a ClusterRole and bind it with a ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to the pod-reader service account didn’t grant permissions on pods. It only allowed list on deployments in the apps API group.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions in the core API group:
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing deployments list rule.

It’s fixed now. Try again.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or run a Pod using serviceAccountName: pod-reader and kubectl get pods in that namespace.

If you need to list pods cluster-wide, we would instead create a ClusterRole and bind it with a ClusterRoleBinding.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to the pod-reader service account didn’t grant permissions on pods. It only allowed list on deployments in the apps API group.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions in the core API group:
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing deployments list rule.

It’s fixed now. Try again.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or run a Pod using serviceAccountName: pod-reader and kubectl get pods in that namespace.

If you need to list pods cluster-wide, we would instead create a ClusterRole and bind it with a ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root causes:
  - Service selector mismatch: Service nginx selected app=web, while the Deployment labels pods with app=nginx. Result: Service had no endpoints.
  - Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80. Even if pods were matched, traffic to port 80 would fail.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080 (Service still exposes port 80)
- Outcome:
  - Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.30:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080
  - In-cluster request returns HTTP 200

Evidence
- Before: Endpoints nginx showed “<none>”; EndpointSlice had no endpoints.
- After:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:8080
  - EndpointSlice: port 8080, endpoint 10.244.0.30
  - From within the nginx pod: curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ → HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes and next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Create a NodePort Service, or
  - Create a LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it), or
  - Create an Ingress (you’ll need an Ingress controller).
- Optional cleanup/improvement:
  - Add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment pod spec (for clarity; not required for functionality).
  - Add readinessProbe on port 8080 to ensure the Service only routes to ready pods.

Tell me if you want me to expose it externally (NodePort/Ingress), and I’ll set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Root causes:
  - Service selector mismatch: Service nginx selected app=web, while the Deployment labels pods with app=nginx. Result: Service had no endpoints.
  - Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80. Even if pods were matched, traffic to port 80 would fail.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080 (Service still exposes port 80)
- Outcome:
  - Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.30:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080
  - In-cluster request returns HTTP 200

Evidence
- Before: Endpoints nginx showed “<none>”; EndpointSlice had no endpoints.
- After:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:8080
  - EndpointSlice: port 8080, endpoint 10.244.0.30
  - From within the nginx pod: curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ → HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes and next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Create a NodePort Service, or
  - Create a LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it), or
  - Create an Ingress (you’ll need an Ingress controller).
- Optional cleanup/improvement:
  - Add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment pod spec (for clarity; not required for functionality).
  - Add readinessProbe on port 8080 to ensure the Service only routes to ready pods.

Tell me if you want me to expose it externally (NodePort/Ingress), and I’ll set it up.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root causes:
  - Service selector mismatch: Service nginx selected app=web, while the Deployment labels pods with app=nginx. Result: Service had no endpoints.
  - Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80. Even if pods were matched, traffic to port 80 would fail.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080 (Service still exposes port 80)
- Outcome:
  - Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.30:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080
  - In-cluster request returns HTTP 200

Evidence
- Before: Endpoints nginx showed “<none>”; EndpointSlice had no endpoints.
- After:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:8080
  - EndpointSlice: port 8080, endpoint 10.244.0.30
  - From within the nginx pod: curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ → HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes and next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Create a NodePort Service, or
  - Create a LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it), or
  - Create an Ingress (you’ll need an Ingress controller).
- Optional cleanup/improvement:
  - Add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment pod spec (for clarity; not required for functionality).
  - Add readinessProbe on port 8080 to ensure the Service only routes to ready pods.

Tell me if you want me to expose it externally (NodePort/Ingress), and I’ll set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Root cause
- The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label. Result: pods stayed Pending (FailedScheduling), so the Service had no endpoints and connections failed.
- The Service was targeting port 80, while the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged defaults to listening on 8080. Even if pods had started, the port mismatch would have caused connection refusals.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector so the pods can schedule on the available node.
- Set the container to expose port 8080 and updated the Service targetPort to 8080.
- Added readiness and liveness probes on / to ensure traffic only reaches ready pods.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running and Ready in namespace webshop-frontend.
  - web-app-deployment-545788b7ff-vcfwj 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-545788b7ff-sb9lj 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints: web-app-service now has endpoints
  - 10.244.0.33:8080, 10.244.0.34:8080

How to verify
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sSI web-app-service
  - You should get HTTP 200 OK headers.
- From another pod/namespace, resolve DNS:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run dns --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- nslookup web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

Notes
- I deleted and recreated the Deployment to remove the stuck nodeSelector cleanly.
- Using nginx-unprivileged on 8080 is the right choice; services should target 8080 in this setup.
- If you later add GPU nodes and truly need node placement, consider:
  - Labeling the intended nodes (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu) and
  - Adding tolerations/affinity properly, plus a fallback or multiple node pools.

If you want, I can pin resource requests/limits and add HorizontalPodAutoscaler next.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Root cause
- The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label. Result: pods stayed Pending (FailedScheduling), so the Service had no endpoints and connections failed.
- The Service was targeting port 80, while the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged defaults to listening on 8080. Even if pods had started, the port mismatch would have caused connection refusals.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector so the pods can schedule on the available node.
- Set the container to expose port 8080 and updated the Service targetPort to 8080.
- Added readiness and liveness probes on / to ensure traffic only reaches ready pods.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running and Ready in namespace webshop-frontend.
  - web-app-deployment-545788b7ff-vcfwj 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-545788b7ff-sb9lj 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints: web-app-service now has endpoints
  - 10.244.0.33:8080, 10.244.0.34:8080

How to verify
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sSI web-app-service
  - You should get HTTP 200 OK headers.
- From another pod/namespace, resolve DNS:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run dns --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- nslookup web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

Notes
- I deleted and recreated the Deployment to remove the stuck nodeSelector cleanly.
- Using nginx-unprivileged on 8080 is the right choice; services should target 8080 in this setup.
- If you later add GPU nodes and truly need node placement, consider:
  - Labeling the intended nodes (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu) and
  - Adding tolerations/affinity properly, plus a fallback or multiple node pools.

If you want, I can pin resource requests/limits and add HorizontalPodAutoscaler next.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

Root cause
- The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label. Result: pods stayed Pending (FailedScheduling), so the Service had no endpoints and connections failed.
- The Service was targeting port 80, while the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged defaults to listening on 8080. Even if pods had started, the port mismatch would have caused connection refusals.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector so the pods can schedule on the available node.
- Set the container to expose port 8080 and updated the Service targetPort to 8080.
- Added readiness and liveness probes on / to ensure traffic only reaches ready pods.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running and Ready in namespace webshop-frontend.
  - web-app-deployment-545788b7ff-vcfwj 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-545788b7ff-sb9lj 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints: web-app-service now has endpoints
  - 10.244.0.33:8080, 10.244.0.34:8080

How to verify
- From inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sSI web-app-service
  - You should get HTTP 200 OK headers.
- From another pod/namespace, resolve DNS:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run dns --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- nslookup web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

Notes
- I deleted and recreated the Deployment to remove the stuck nodeSelector cleanly.
- Using nginx-unprivileged on 8080 is the right choice; services should target 8080 in this setup.
- If you later add GPU nodes and truly need node placement, consider:
  - Labeling the intended nodes (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu) and
  - Adding tolerations/affinity properly, plus a fallback or multiple node pools.

If you want, I can pin resource requests/limits and add HorizontalPodAutoscaler next.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I configured the cluster to meet your requirements. Summary of what’s in place and how it enforces least privilege and isolation:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels used for policy selection:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: tenant=dev, owner=<name>, access=developer
  - dev-shared: tenant=dev, shared=true, access=developer
  - staging: env=staging, access=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access=restricted

2) RBAC
- Per-developer admin in their namespace:
  - RoleBindings (to ClusterRole=admin) in each of dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie for the corresponding User (alice, bob, charlie) and ServiceAccount (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa).
  - ServiceAccounts created: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie).
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole=view to Users alice, bob, charlie and their ServiceAccounts.
- Staging/prod access restricted:
  - No RoleBindings created for developers in staging or prod. Access is implicitly limited to cluster-admins (RBAC is additive, no grants = no access). If you use custom groups, ensure none are bound there.

Notes:
- User identities alice/bob/charlie assume your auth (OIDC/certs/SSO) maps those usernames to kube subjects.
- If you ever prefer “edit” (no RBAC management) instead of “admin,” delete and recreate the RoleBindings (roleRef is immutable).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (dev-quota):
  - cpu: requests=2, limits=2
  - memory: requests=4Gi, limits=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared (dev-shared-quota):
  - cpu: requests=4, limits=4
  - memory: requests=8Gi, limits=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod (env-quota):
  - cpu: requests=8, limits=8
  - memory: requests=16Gi, limits=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces): In all six namespaces, default-deny-all for Ingress and Egress.
- Allow same-namespace traffic (east-west within namespace): allow-same-namespace in each namespace for both Ingress and Egress.
- Allow DNS egress to kube-dns: allow-dns-egress in each namespace (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system). This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” minimally (DNS). If you also want pods to reach the Kubernetes API service (default/kubernetes:443) or other system endpoints, say the word and I’ll add narrowly-scoped rules.
- Developer access limited to own ns and dev-shared; cross-developer blocked:
  - From each developer ns: allow-to-dev-shared (egress only) to namespaceSelector name=dev-shared.
  - In dev-shared: allow-from-dev-namespaces (ingress) from namespaces with label owner in [alice, bob, charlie].
  - No policies allow traffic between dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie directly.
- Staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - Only same-namespace traffic + DNS. No rules allow any dev namespace to reach staging/prod or vice versa.

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented in all dev and env namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod). No changes made to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system).

How this meets your requirements
- Separation: Dedicated namespaces per developer plus shared and environment namespaces created.
- Least privilege: Developers have full control only in their own namespace; read-only in dev-shared; no access to staging/prod. Service accounts mirror the same privileges.
- Quotas enforce resource ceilings as specified.
- Network isolation: Default deny + same-namespace only + explicit dev-to-shared path prevents cross-tenant leakage and isolates staging/prod from dev.

Optional next steps (tell me if you want these applied)
- LimitRanges to enforce per-pod default requests/limits consistent with quotas (prevents accidental quota starvation).
- NetworkPolicy to allow egress to the Kubernetes API service (443 in default namespace) if your workloads need in-cluster API access.
- External egress policies (egress to internet, artifact registries, etc.) scoped to required destinations.
- Pod Security admission/constraints (Baseline/Restricted) per namespace for stronger workload hardening.
- Resource requests/limits guardrails via ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

Verification quick checks
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC in a dev ns: kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota dev-quota
- Netpol: kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy
- Access test (example): try kubectl -n dev-shared get pods as alice (should read), and kubectl -n staging get pods (should be forbidden)

If you want a single consolidated manifest for GitOps, I can generate one from the live state.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I configured the cluster to meet your requirements. Summary of what’s in place and how it enforces least privilege and isolation:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels used for policy selection:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: tenant=dev, owner=<name>, access=developer
  - dev-shared: tenant=dev, shared=true, access=developer
  - staging: env=staging, access=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access=restricted

2) RBAC
- Per-developer admin in their namespace:
  - RoleBindings (to ClusterRole=admin) in each of dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie for the corresponding User (alice, bob, charlie) and ServiceAccount (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa).
  - ServiceAccounts created: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie).
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole=view to Users alice, bob, charlie and their ServiceAccounts.
- Staging/prod access restricted:
  - No RoleBindings created for developers in staging or prod. Access is implicitly limited to cluster-admins (RBAC is additive, no grants = no access). If you use custom groups, ensure none are bound there.

Notes:
- User identities alice/bob/charlie assume your auth (OIDC/certs/SSO) maps those usernames to kube subjects.
- If you ever prefer “edit” (no RBAC management) instead of “admin,” delete and recreate the RoleBindings (roleRef is immutable).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (dev-quota):
  - cpu: requests=2, limits=2
  - memory: requests=4Gi, limits=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared (dev-shared-quota):
  - cpu: requests=4, limits=4
  - memory: requests=8Gi, limits=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod (env-quota):
  - cpu: requests=8, limits=8
  - memory: requests=16Gi, limits=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces): In all six namespaces, default-deny-all for Ingress and Egress.
- Allow same-namespace traffic (east-west within namespace): allow-same-namespace in each namespace for both Ingress and Egress.
- Allow DNS egress to kube-dns: allow-dns-egress in each namespace (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system). This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” minimally (DNS). If you also want pods to reach the Kubernetes API service (default/kubernetes:443) or other system endpoints, say the word and I’ll add narrowly-scoped rules.
- Developer access limited to own ns and dev-shared; cross-developer blocked:
  - From each developer ns: allow-to-dev-shared (egress only) to namespaceSelector name=dev-shared.
  - In dev-shared: allow-from-dev-namespaces (ingress) from namespaces with label owner in [alice, bob, charlie].
  - No policies allow traffic between dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie directly.
- Staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - Only same-namespace traffic + DNS. No rules allow any dev namespace to reach staging/prod or vice versa.

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented in all dev and env namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod). No changes made to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system).

How this meets your requirements
- Separation: Dedicated namespaces per developer plus shared and environment namespaces created.
- Least privilege: Developers have full control only in their own namespace; read-only in dev-shared; no access to staging/prod. Service accounts mirror the same privileges.
- Quotas enforce resource ceilings as specified.
- Network isolation: Default deny + same-namespace only + explicit dev-to-shared path prevents cross-tenant leakage and isolates staging/prod from dev.

Optional next steps (tell me if you want these applied)
- LimitRanges to enforce per-pod default requests/limits consistent with quotas (prevents accidental quota starvation).
- NetworkPolicy to allow egress to the Kubernetes API service (443 in default namespace) if your workloads need in-cluster API access.
- External egress policies (egress to internet, artifact registries, etc.) scoped to required destinations.
- Pod Security admission/constraints (Baseline/Restricted) per namespace for stronger workload hardening.
- Resource requests/limits guardrails via ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

Verification quick checks
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC in a dev ns: kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota dev-quota
- Netpol: kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy
- Access test (example): try kubectl -n dev-shared get pods as alice (should read), and kubectl -n staging get pods (should be forbidden)

If you want a single consolidated manifest for GitOps, I can generate one from the live state.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I configured the cluster to meet your requirements. Summary of what’s in place and how it enforces least privilege and isolation:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels used for policy selection:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: tenant=dev, owner=<name>, access=developer
  - dev-shared: tenant=dev, shared=true, access=developer
  - staging: env=staging, access=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access=restricted

2) RBAC
- Per-developer admin in their namespace:
  - RoleBindings (to ClusterRole=admin) in each of dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie for the corresponding User (alice, bob, charlie) and ServiceAccount (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa).
  - ServiceAccounts created: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie).
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole=view to Users alice, bob, charlie and their ServiceAccounts.
- Staging/prod access restricted:
  - No RoleBindings created for developers in staging or prod. Access is implicitly limited to cluster-admins (RBAC is additive, no grants = no access). If you use custom groups, ensure none are bound there.

Notes:
- User identities alice/bob/charlie assume your auth (OIDC/certs/SSO) maps those usernames to kube subjects.
- If you ever prefer “edit” (no RBAC management) instead of “admin,” delete and recreate the RoleBindings (roleRef is immutable).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (dev-quota):
  - cpu: requests=2, limits=2
  - memory: requests=4Gi, limits=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared (dev-shared-quota):
  - cpu: requests=4, limits=4
  - memory: requests=8Gi, limits=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod (env-quota):
  - cpu: requests=8, limits=8
  - memory: requests=16Gi, limits=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces): In all six namespaces, default-deny-all for Ingress and Egress.
- Allow same-namespace traffic (east-west within namespace): allow-same-namespace in each namespace for both Ingress and Egress.
- Allow DNS egress to kube-dns: allow-dns-egress in each namespace (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system). This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” minimally (DNS). If you also want pods to reach the Kubernetes API service (default/kubernetes:443) or other system endpoints, say the word and I’ll add narrowly-scoped rules.
- Developer access limited to own ns and dev-shared; cross-developer blocked:
  - From each developer ns: allow-to-dev-shared (egress only) to namespaceSelector name=dev-shared.
  - In dev-shared: allow-from-dev-namespaces (ingress) from namespaces with label owner in [alice, bob, charlie].
  - No policies allow traffic between dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie directly.
- Staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - Only same-namespace traffic + DNS. No rules allow any dev namespace to reach staging/prod or vice versa.

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented in all dev and env namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod). No changes made to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system).

How this meets your requirements
- Separation: Dedicated namespaces per developer plus shared and environment namespaces created.
- Least privilege: Developers have full control only in their own namespace; read-only in dev-shared; no access to staging/prod. Service accounts mirror the same privileges.
- Quotas enforce resource ceilings as specified.
- Network isolation: Default deny + same-namespace only + explicit dev-to-shared path prevents cross-tenant leakage and isolates staging/prod from dev.

Optional next steps (tell me if you want these applied)
- LimitRanges to enforce per-pod default requests/limits consistent with quotas (prevents accidental quota starvation).
- NetworkPolicy to allow egress to the Kubernetes API service (443 in default namespace) if your workloads need in-cluster API access.
- External egress policies (egress to internet, artifact registries, etc.) scoped to required destinations.
- Pod Security admission/constraints (Baseline/Restricted) per namespace for stronger workload hardening.
- Resource requests/limits guardrails via ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

- Created namespace: statefulset-test

This field is immutable. It can only be set for containers.

items.description: ResourceClaim references one entry in PodSpec.ResourceClaims.

Name must match the name of one entry in pod.spec.resourceClaims of
the Pod where this field is used. It makes that resource available
inside a container.

request.description:
Request is the name chosen for a request in the referenced claim.
If empty, everything from the claim is made available, otherwise
only the result of this request.

Limits describes the maximum amount of compute resources allowed.
More info: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/

If Requests is omitted for a container, it defaults to Limits if that is explicitly specified,
otherwise to an implementation-defined value. Requests cannot exceed Limits.

privileges than its parent process. This bool directly controls if
the no_new_privs flag will be set on the container process.
AllowPrivilegeEscalation is true always when the container is:
1) run as Privileged
2) has CAP_SYS_ADMIN
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

appArmorProfile.description:
appArmorProfile is the AppArmor options to use by this container. If set, this profile
overrides the pod's appArmorProfile.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

localhostProfile.description:
localhostProfile indicates a profile loaded on the node that should be used.
The profile must be preconfigured on the node to work.
Must match the loaded name of the profile.
Must be set if and only if type is "Localhost".

type.description:
type indicates which kind of AppArmor profile will be applied.
Valid options are:
  Localhost - a profile pre-loaded on the node.
  RuntimeDefault - the container runtime's default profile.
  Unconfined - no AppArmor enforcement.

Defaults to the default set of capabilities granted by the container runtime.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

items.description: Capability represent POSIX capabilities type
Capability represent POSIX capabilities type

privileged.description:
Run container in privileged mode.
Processes in privileged containers are essentially equivalent to root on the host.
Defaults to false.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

procMount.description:
procMount denotes the type of proc mount to use for the containers.
The default value is Default which uses the container runtime defaults for
readonly paths and masked paths.
This requires the ProcMountType feature flag to be enabled.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

readOnlyRootFilesystem.description:
Whether this container has a read-only root filesystem.
Default is false.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

runAsGroup.description:
The GID to run the entrypoint of the container process.
Uses runtime default if unset.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

runAsNonRoot.description:
Indicates that the container must run as a non-root user.
If true, the Kubelet will validate the image at runtime to ensure that it
does not run as UID 0 (root) and fail to start the container if it does.
If unset or false, no such validation will be performed.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.

runAsUser.description:
The UID to run the entrypoint of the container process.
Defaults to user specified in image metadata if unspecified.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

seLinuxOptions.description:
The SELinux context to be applied to the container.
If unspecified, the container runtime will allocate a random SELinux context for each
container.  May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

level.description: Level is SELinux level label that applies to the container.

role.description: Role is a SELinux role label that applies to the container.

type.description: Type is a SELinux type label that applies to the container.

user.description: User is a SELinux user label that applies to the container.

seccompProfile.description:

provided at both the pod & container level, the container options
override the pod options.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

localhostProfile.description:
localhostProfile indicates a profile defined in a file on the node should be used.
The profile must be preconfigured on the node to work.
Must be a descending path, relative to the kubelet's configured seccomp profile location.
Must be set if type is "Localhost". Must NOT be set for any other type.

type.description:
type indicates which kind of seccomp profile will be applied.
Valid options are:

Localhost - a profile defined in a file on the node should be used.
RuntimeDefault - the container runtime default profile should be used.
Unconfined - no profile should be applied.

windowsOptions.description:
The Windows specific settings applied to all containers.
If unspecified, the options from the PodSecurityContext will be used.
If set in both SecurityContext and PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is linux.

mountPropagation.description:
mountPropagation determines how mounts are propagated from the host
to container and the other way around.
When not set, MountPropagationNone is used.
This field is beta in 1.10.
When RecursiveReadOnly is set to IfPossible or to Enabled, MountPropagation must be None or unspecified
(which defaults to None).

name.description: This must match the Name of a Volume.

readOnly.description:
Mounted read-only if true, read-write otherwise (false or unspecified).
Defaults to false.

recursiveReadOnly.description:
RecursiveReadOnly specifies whether read-only mounts should be handled
recursively.

If ReadOnly is false, this field has no meaning and must be unspecified.

If ReadOnly is true, and this field is set to Disabled, the mount is not made
recursively read-only.  If this field is set to IfPossible, the mount is made
recursively read-only, if it is supported by the container runtime.  If this
field is set to Enabled, the mount is made recursively read-only if it is
supported by the container runtime, otherwise the pod will not be started and
an error will be generated to indicate the reason.

If this field is set to IfPossible or Enabled, MountPropagation must be set to
None (or be unspecified, which defaults to None).

If this field is not specified, it is treated as an equivalent of Disabled.

claims.description:
Claims lists the names of resources, defined in spec.resourceClaims,
that are used by this container.

This field depends on the
DynamicResourceAllocation feature gate.

This field is immutable. It can only be set for containers.

items.description: ResourceClaim references one entry in PodSpec.ResourceClaims.

name.description:
Name must match the name of one entry in pod.spec.resourceClaims of
the Pod where this field is used. It makes that resource available
inside a container.

request.description:
Request is the name chosen for a request in the referenced claim.
If empty, everything from the claim is made available, otherwise
only the result of this request.

limits.description:
Limits describes the maximum amount of compute resources allowed.
More info: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/

requests.description:
Requests describes the minimum amount of compute resources required.
If Requests is omitted for a container, it defaults to Limits if that is explicitly specified,
otherwise to an implementation-defined value. Requests cannot exceed Limits.
More info: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/

allowPrivilegeEscalation.description:
AllowPrivilegeEscalation controls whether a process can gain more
privileges than its parent process. This bool directly controls if
the no_new_privs flag will be set on the container process.
AllowPrivilegeEscalation is true always when the container is:
1) run as Privileged
2) has CAP_SYS_ADMIN
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

appArmorProfile.description:
appArmorProfile is the AppArmor options to use by this container. If set, this profile
overrides the pod's appArmorProfile.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

localhostProfile.description:
localhostProfile indicates a profile loaded on the node that should be used.
The profile must be preconfigured on the node to work.
Must match the loaded name of the profile.
Must be set if and only if type is "Localhost".

type.description:
type indicates which kind of AppArmor profile will be applied.
Valid options are:
  Localhost - a profile pre-loaded on the node.
  RuntimeDefault - the container runtime's default profile.
  Unconfined - no AppArmor enforcement.

capabilities.description:
The capabilities to add/drop when running containers.
Defaults to the default set of capabilities granted by the container runtime.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

items.description: Capability represent POSIX capabilities type
Capability represent POSIX capabilities type

privileged.description:
Run container in privileged mode.
Processes in privileged containers are essentially equivalent to root on the host.
Defaults to false.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

procMount.description:
procMount denotes the type of proc mount to use for the containers.
The default value is Default which uses the container runtime defaults for
readonly paths and masked paths.
This requires the ProcMountType feature flag to be enabled.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

readOnlyRootFilesystem.description:
Whether this container has a read-only root filesystem.
Default is false.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

runAsGroup.description:
The GID to run the entrypoint of the container process.
Uses runtime default if unset.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

runAsNonRoot.description:
Indicates that the container must run as a non-root user.
If true, the Kubelet will validate the image at runtime to ensure that it
does not run as UID 0 (root) and fail to start the container if it does.
If unset or false, no such validation will be performed.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.

runAsUser.description:
The UID to run the entrypoint of the container process.
Defaults to user specified in image metadata if unspecified.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

seLinuxOptions.description:
The SELinux context to be applied to the container.
If unspecified, the container runtime will allocate a random SELinux context for each
container.  May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

level.description: Level is SELinux level label that applies to the container.

role.description: Role is a SELinux role label that applies to the container.

type.description: Type is a SELinux type label that applies to the container.

user.description: User is a SELinux user label that applies to the container.

seccompProfile.description:
The seccomp options to use by this container. If seccomp options are
provided at both the pod & container level, the container options
override the pod options.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

localhostProfile.description:
localhostProfile indicates a profile defined in a file on the node should be used.
The profile must be preconfigured on the node to work.
Must be a descending path, relative to the kubelet's configured seccomp profile location.
Must be set if type is "Localhost". Must NOT be set for any other type.

type.description:
type indicates which kind of seccomp profile will be applied.
Valid options are:

Localhost - a profile defined in a file on the node should be used.
RuntimeDefault - the container runtime default profile should be used.
Unconfined - no profile should be applied.

windowsOptions.description:
The Windows specific settings applied to all containers.
If unspecified, the options from the PodSecurityContext will be used.
If set in both SecurityContext and PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is linux.

gmsaCredentialSpec.description:
GMSACredentialSpec is where the GMSA admission webhook
(https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/windows-gmsa) inlines the contents of the
GMSA credential spec named by the GMSACredentialSpecName field.

gmsaCredentialSpecName.description: GMSACredentialSpecName is the name of the GMSA credential spec to use.

hostProcess.description:
HostProcess determines if a container should be run as a 'Host Process' container.
All of a Pod's containers must have the same effective HostProcess value
(it is not allowed to have a mix of HostProcess containers and non-HostProcess containers).
In addition, if HostProcess is true then HostNetwork must also be set to true.

runAsUserName.description:
The UserName in Windows to run the entrypoint of the container process.
Defaults to the user specified in image metadata if unspecified.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext. If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.

items.description: volumeDevice describes a mapping of a raw block device within a container.

devicePath.description: devicePath is the path inside of the container that the device will be mapped to.

name.description: name must match the name of a persistentVolumeClaim in the pod

items.description: VolumeMount describes a mounting of a Volume within a container.

mountPath.description:
Path within the container at which the volume should be mounted.  Must
not contain ':'.

mountPropagation.description:
mountPropagation determines how mounts are propagated from the host
to container and the other way around.
When not set, MountPropagationNone is used.
This field is beta in 1.10.
When RecursiveReadOnly is set to IfPossible or to Enabled, MountPropagation must be None or unspecified
(which defaults to None).

name.description: This must match the Name of a Volume.

readOnly.description:
Mounted read-only if true, read-write otherwise (false or unspecified).
Defaults to false.

recursiveReadOnly.description:
RecursiveReadOnly specifies whether read-only mounts should be handled
recursively.

If ReadOnly is false, this field has no meaning and must be unspecified.

If ReadOnly is true, and this field is set to Disabled, the mount is not made
recursively read-only.  If this field is set to IfPossible, the mount is made
recursively read-only, if it is supported by the container runtime.  If this
field is set to Enabled, the mount is made recursively read-only if it is
supported by the container runtime, otherwise the pod will not be started and
an error will be generated to indicate the reason.

If this field is set to IfPossible or Enabled, MountPropagation must be set to
None (or be unspecified, which defaults to None).

If this field is not specified, it is treated as an equivalent of Disabled.

subPath.description:
Path within the volume from which the container's volume should be mounted.
Defaults to "" (volume's root).

subPathExpr.description:
Expanded path within the volume from which the container's volume should be mounted.
Behaves similarly to SubPath but environment variable references $(VAR_NAME) are expanded using the container's environment.
Defaults to "" (volume's root).
SubPathExpr and SubPath are mutually exclusive.

items.description: Step

command.description: Command

items.description: EnvVar represents an environment variable present in a Container.

name.description:
Name of the environment variable.
May consist of any printable ASCII characters except '='.

value.description:
Variable references $(VAR_NAME) are expanded
using the previously defined environment variables in the container and
any service environment variables. If a variable cannot be resolved,
the reference in the input string will be unchanged. Double $$ are reduced
to a single $, which allows for escaping the $(VAR_NAME) syntax: i.e.
"$$(VAR_NAME)" will produce the string literal "$(VAR_NAME)".
Escaped references will never be expanded, regardless of whether the variable
exists or not.
Defaults to "".

valueFrom.description: Source for the environment variable's value. Cannot be used if value is not empty.

configMapKeyRef.description: Selects a key of a ConfigMap.

name.description:
Name of the referent.
This field is effectively required, but due to backwards compatibility is
allowed to be empty. Instances of this type with an empty value here are
almost certainly wrong.
More info: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names/#names

optional.description: Specify whether the ConfigMap or its key must be defined

fieldRef.description:
Selects a field of the pod: supports metadata.name, metadata.namespace, `metadata.labels['<KEY>']`, `metadata.annotations['<KEY>']`,
spec.nodeName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.hostIP, status.podIP, status.podIPs.

apiVersion.description: Version of the schema the FieldPath is written in terms of, defaults to "v1".

fieldPath.description: Path of the field to select in the specified API version.

fileKeyRef.description:
FileKeyRef selects a key of the env file.
Requires the EnvFiles feature gate to be enabled.

key.description:
The key within the env file. An invalid key will prevent the pod from starting.
The keys defined within a source may consist of any printable ASCII characters except '='.
During Alpha stage of the EnvFiles feature gate, the key size is limited to 128 characters.

optional.description:
Specify whether the file or its key must be defined. If the file or key
does not exist, then the env var is not published.
If optional is set to true and the specified key does not exist,
the environment variable will not be set in the Pod's containers.

If optional is set to false and the specified key does not exist,
an error will be returned during Pod creation.

path.description:
The path within the volume from which to select the file.
Must be relative and may not contain the '..' path or start with '..'.

volumeName.description: The name of the volume mount containing the env file.

resourceFieldRef.description:
Selects a resource of the container: only resources limits and requests
(limits.cpu, limits.memory, limits.ephemeral-storage, requests.cpu, requests.memory and requests.ephemeral-storage) are currently supported.

preStop.description:
PreStop is called immediately before a container is terminated due to an
API request or management event such as liveness/startup probe failure,
preemption, resource contention, etc. The handler is not called if the
container crashes or exits. The Pod's termination grace period countdown begins before the
PreStop hook is executed. Regardless of the outcome of the handler, the
container will eventually terminate within the Pod's termination grace
period (unless delayed by finalizers). Other management of the container blocks until the hook completes
or until the termination grace period is reached.
More info: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/#container-hooks

that are used by this container.

This field is immutable. It can only be set for containers.

the Pod where this field is used. It makes that resource available
inside a container.

Request is the name chosen for a request in the referenced claim.
If empty, everything from the claim is made available, otherwise
only the result of this request.

If Requests is omitted for a container, it defaults to Limits if that is explicitly specified,
otherwise to an implementation-defined value. Requests cannot exceed Limits.

Used to distinguish between a single string and an array of strings.

properties.description: Properties is the JSON Schema properties to support key-value pairs results.

type.description: The possible types are 'string', 'array', and 'object', with 'string' as the default.

allowPrivilegeEscalation.description:
AllowPrivilegeEscalation controls whether a process can gain more
privileges than its parent process. This bool directly controls if
the no_new_privs flag will be set on the container process.
AllowPrivilegeEscalation is true always when the container is:
1) run as Privileged
2) has CAP_SYS_ADMIN
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

appArmorProfile.description:
appArmorProfile is the AppArmor options to use by this container. If set, this profile
overrides the pod's appArmorProfile.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

localhostProfile.description:
localhostProfile indicates a profile loaded on the node that should be used.
The profile must be preconfigured on the node to work.
Must match the loaded name of the profile.
Must be set if and only if type is "Localhost".

type.description:
type indicates which kind of AppArmor profile will be applied.
Valid options are:
  Localhost - a profile pre-loaded on the node.
  RuntimeDefault - the container runtime's default profile.
  Unconfined - no AppArmor enforcement.

capabilities.description:
The capabilities to add/drop when running containers.
Defaults to the default set of capabilities granted by the container runtime.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

items.description: Capability represent POSIX capabilities type
Capability represent POSIX capabilities type

privileged.description:
Run container in privileged mode.
Processes in privileged containers are essentially equivalent to root on the host.
Defaults to false.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

procMount.description:
procMount denotes the type of proc mount to use for the containers.
The default value is Default which uses the container runtime defaults for
readonly paths and masked paths.
This requires the ProcMountType feature flag to be enabled.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

readOnlyRootFilesystem.description:
Whether this container has a read-only root filesystem.
Default is false.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

runAsGroup.description:
The GID to run the entrypoint of the container process.
Uses runtime default if unset.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

runAsNonRoot.description:
Indicates that the container must run as a non-root user.
If true, the Kubelet will validate the image at runtime to ensure that it
does not run as UID 0 (root) and fail to start the container if it does.
If unset or false, no such validation will be performed.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.

runAsUser.description:
The UID to run the entrypoint of the container process.
Defaults to user specified in image metadata if unspecified.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

seLinuxOptions.description:
The SELinux context to be applied to the container.
If unspecified, the container runtime will allocate a random SELinux context for each
container.  May also be set in PodSecurityContext.  If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

level.description: Level is SELinux level label that applies to the container.

role.description: Role is a SELinux role label that applies to the container.

type.description: Type is a SELinux type label that applies to the container.

user.description: User is a SELinux user label that applies to the container.

seccompProfile.description:
The seccomp options to use by this container. If seccomp options are
provided at both the pod & container level, the container options
override the pod options.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is windows.

localhostProfile.description:
localhostProfile indicates a profile defined in a file on the node should be used.
The profile must be preconfigured on the node to work.
Must be a descending path, relative to the kubelet's configured seccomp profile location.
Must be set if type is "Localhost". Must NOT be set for any other type.

type.description:
type indicates which kind of seccomp profile will be applied.
Valid options are:

Localhost - a profile defined in a file on the node should be used.
RuntimeDefault - the container runtime default profile should be used.
Unconfined - no profile should be applied.

windowsOptions.description:
The Windows specific settings applied to all containers.
If unspecified, the options from the PodSecurityContext will be used.
If set in both SecurityContext and PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.
Note that this field cannot be set when spec.os.name is linux.

gmsaCredentialSpec.description:
GMSACredentialSpec is where the GMSA admission webhook
(https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/windows-gmsa) inlines the contents of the
GMSA credential spec named by the GMSACredentialSpecName field.

gmsaCredentialSpecName.description: GMSACredentialSpecName is the name of the GMSA credential spec to use.

hostProcess.description:
HostProcess determines if a container should be run as a 'Host Process' container.
All of a Pod's containers must have the same effective HostProcess value
(it is not allowed to have a mix of HostProcess containers and non-HostProcess containers).
In addition, if HostProcess is true then HostNetwork must also be set to true.

runAsUserName.description:
The UserName in Windows to run the entrypoint of the container process.
Defaults to the user specified in image metadata if unspecified.
May also be set in PodSecurityContext. If set in both SecurityContext and
PodSecurityContext, the value specified in SecurityContext takes precedence.

items.description: volumeDevice describes a mapping of a raw block device within a container.

devicePath.description: devicePath is the path inside of the container that the device will be mapped to.

items.description: VolumeMount describes a mounting of a Volume within a container.

mountPath.description:
Path within the container at which the volume should be mounted.  Must
not contain ':'.

mountPropagation.description:
mountPropagation determines how mounts are propagated from the host
to container and the other way around.
When not set, MountPropagationNone is used.
This field is beta in 1.10.
When RecursiveReadOnly is set to IfPossible or to Enabled, MountPropagation must be None or unspecified
(which defaults to None).

name.description: This must match the Name of a Volume.

readOnly.description:
Mounted read-only if true, read-write otherwise (false or unspecified).
Defaults to false.

recursiveReadOnly.description:
RecursiveReadOnly specifies whether read-only mounts should be handled
recursively.

If ReadOnly is false, this field has no meaning and must be unspecified.

If ReadOnly is true, and this field is set to Disabled, the mount is not made
recursively read-only.  If this field is set to IfPossible, the mount is made
recursively read-only, if it is supported by the container runtime.  If this
field is set to Enabled, the mount is made recursively read-only if it is
supported by the container runtime, otherwise the pod will not be started and
an error will be generated to indicate the reason.

If this field is set to IfPossible or Enabled, MountPropagation must be set to
None (or be unspecified, which defaults to None).

If this field is not specified, it is treated as an equivalent of Disabled.

subPath.description:
Path within the volume from which the container's volume should be mounted.
Defaults to "" (volume's root).

subPathExpr.description:
Expanded path within the volume from which the container's volume should be mounted.
Behaves similarly to SubPath but environment variable references $(VAR_NAME) are expanded using the container's environment.
Defaults to "" (volume's root).
SubPathExpr and SubPath are mutually exclusive.
